# Introduction

Artificial intelligence has undergone a paradigmatic shift over the past two decades, transitioning (from {rule-based [expert (systems [to] deep) networks}] and encompassing) a far broader methodological landscape that now spans reinforcement learning, large-scale language modeling, and multimodal generative architectures. This proliferation of approaches has, in turn, generated an urgent need for unified theoretical frameworks capable of addressing questions of interpretability, robustness, and alignment that no single subfield can resolve in isolation.

The central concern of this paper is what we term *architectural coherence*: the degree to which disparate components of a composite AI system (e.g., {perception [modules (whose [internal] representations) are trained via] adversarial objectives}) interact in ways that preserve the system's global decision-theoretic guarantees. We argue that without explicit attention to such coherence, the modular composition strategies popular in current industrial pipelines risk accumulating emergent failure modes that are invisible to any single component's test suite.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we formalize a layered compositional semantics for hybrid neuro-symbolic pipelines. Second, we derive sufficient conditions under which end-to-end training objectives remain stable across architectural modifications. Third, we demonstrate—through both theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation on a suite of multi-task benchmarks—that the proposed conditions reduce worst-case error propagation by a factor of 3.2 relative to standard modular fine-tuning baselines. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related work; Section 3 develops the formalism; Section 4 presents experiments; and Section 5 discusses limitations and avenues for future research.
